title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Part 1
subtitle: Start Here: How to Use This Book, A Note on the Text, the Reader's Charter, and the Prologue
description:
Jubilees counts: seven years make a week, seven weeks make a jubilee, forty-nine years in all. Who counts the days decides what is remembered.

This is Start Here, the opening part of Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration. It gathers everything that comes before Part One: how the book is built, which translation it prints and how it quotes it, the Reader’s Charter, and the Prologue, which reads the story of Noah, Ham and Canaan, including a line Jubilees adds that Genesis does not have (7:13).

Inside this part

  • How to Use This Book — the marked pages (the count line, the witness strip, “Genesis Beside It,” “Where the English Leaves the Ge’ez” and more), three commitments, and a note on what to do when a passage is hard.
  • A Note on the Text — what the Reading Text is, how Charles’s marks are kept, and what this edition changes.
  • The Reader’s Charter — six lines, each earned from the chapters named beneath it.
  • Prologue: The Displeasure of Ham — states the claim of the book in four parts (Kept, Kin in reading on both sides of the line, Heard after the break, and Renewed), four things the book does and four refusals this study holds itself to.

An honest edition

This is a pre-publication manuscript (v0.9, October 2026). The Reading Text is R. H. Charles’s English translation of Jubilees (1902; SPCK 1917), made from the Ethiopic and in the public domain; it is not a new translation and not an official text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The book itself says that no reader of Ge’ez has yet checked this English against the manuscripts and that no specialist in Second Temple Judaism has yet read the commentary; its Foundation Ledger records what has and has not been checked. It is an independent work of study and does not speak for any church.

Digital edition (PDF), 29 pages. Instant access from your Account page after purchase. This is part 1 of 5 of a 373-page volume (pages 7–29 of the complete book, plus cover and front matter).

title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Part 2
subtitle: Booklet 1 of 3: Coming to the Book, Counted, and Allotted (Jubilees 1-10)
description:
Which jubilee are you carrying in your head, and where did you get it? Who decided how the days would be counted, and who drew the line?

This part holds Parts One, Two and Three of the study (Chapters 1–12, with passages from Jubilees 1–10). Part One asks what the word “jubilee” means inside this book and whose hands made the English you read. Part Two, Counted, begins on a mountain with a command to write. Part Three, Allotted, reads a vineyard, a curse and the division of the earth.

Inside this part

  • Part One: Coming to the Book — “Which Jubilee?”, “The Only Whole Book” and “Whose Text Are We Reading?”
  • Part Two: Counted, From Sinai to the Rainbow — “The Angel Is Told to Write,” “The Sabbath Before Israel,” “The Garden as Sanctuary,” “The First Scribe,” “The Flood as Record” and “The Year That Must Not Drift.”
  • Part Three: Allotted — “Noah’s Vineyard and Ham’s Dissent,” “The Lots of the Earth” and “Where Canaan Settled.”
  • The Reading Text — passages from Jubilees 1-10 in R. H. Charles’s translation, set beside the commentary.

A note on care

Part Two includes two hard laws, a Sabbath law that ends in death and a law that counts a mother’s days of uncleanness twice as long when the child is a daughter, and Chapters 10 and 12 read verses that have been used to hurt people. Each chapter tells you so before it begins, and you may stop wherever you need to.

title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Part 3
subtitle: Booklet 2 of 3: Written: Abraham, Jacob, and the Tablets (Jubilees 11-38)
description:
What does a family hand on when it hands on books? Who is written into the covenant, and who is written out?

This part holds Parts Four and Five of the study (Chapters 13–24, with passages from Jubilees 11–38). Part Four follows one man across the line drawn in his own time. Part Five follows the children: a birthright, a blessing, twelve sons, a daughter taken, seven tablets shown at Bethel, a brother sold, and the long quarrel between Jacob’s house and his twin’s.

Inside this part

  • Part Four: Written, Abraham and the Books of the Fathers — “The Boy Who Broke the Idols,” “Two Covenants,” “The Egyptian Woman in the Wilderness,” “The Binding,” “The Cave, the Deed, and the Blessing” and “Abraham’s Last Words.”
  • Part Five: Written, Jacob, Levi, and the Tablets — “The Wells and the Blessing,” “Two Wives, Twelve Sons,” “Dinah, and What Jubilees Did with Her,” “Bethel: Levi, Judah, and the Tablets,” “A Sold Brother, a Dying Mother” and “The Brother Outside the Tower.”
  • The Reading Text — passages from Jubilees 11-38 in R. H. Charles’s translation, with “Genesis Beside It” tables where the book keeps, adds or changes the Genesis story.

A note on care

Chapters 14 to 18 in Part Four and Chapters 19, 21 and 24 in Part Five ask for care. Each tells you where it is going before it goes there, and each lets you stop.

title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Part 4
subtitle: Booklet 3 of 3: Joseph, the Fiftieth Year, and After the Last Page (Jubilees 39-50)
description:
What gets written down when a family is taken apart? What does a people keep when it comes out of bondage and stands at the edge of a land?

This part holds Parts Six, Seven and Eight of the study (Chapters 25–33, with passages from Jubilees 39–50). Part Six follows Joseph into Egypt and the books handed on to Levi. Part Seven follows the people out to the edge of a land, with a sum and a law. Part Eight has no new Reading Text: it steps back from the last page and asks what the book leaves in our hands.

Inside this part

  • Part Six: Written, Joseph, Egypt, and the Books for Levi — “The House of the Egyptian” and “Down to Egypt, and the Books to Levi.”
  • Part Seven: Renewed, The Fiftieth Year — “The Night of the Fourteenth” and “The Fiftieth Year.”
  • Part Eight: After the Last Page — “The Church That Kept the Book of Division,” “Africa in the Book, and the Book in Africa,” “Reading From Both Sides of the Line,” “Five Things to Carry” and “What Jubilees Leaves Us.”
  • The Reading Text — passages from Jubilees 39-50 in R. H. Charles’s translation, set beside the commentary.

A note on care

Chapters 25, 26 and 27 ask for care. In Part Eight, Chapters 29 and 30 often say that the author does not know something, because the people who do are not the people writing this book. Nothing later depends on finishing in one sitting.

title: Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration - Part 5
subtitle: Back Matter: Appendices, Glossary, Bibliography, and Index
description:
The reference shelf of the study: an atlas of the fifty chapters, a timeline, a ledger of every claim and a guide to the sources.

This part holds everything that comes after the last chapter of Jubilees: Covenant, Sacred Time, and Restoration. It is a reference booklet: its entries point back to chapters and pages in the other parts, so it is most useful beside the main text.

Inside this part

  • Appendix A: An Atlas of the Book — the fifty chapters of Jubilees, where each stretch is read in the study, and which ancient witnesses preserve it.
  • Appendix B: Where the English Leaves the Ge’ez — the departures noted in the chapters, gathered into one table.
  • Appendix C: A Timeline — from the composition of the book to the present, with its keepers and its Black American readers side by side.
  • Appendix D: The Foundation Ledger — what each kind of claim rests on, how far it has been checked, and what is still open before print.
  • Appendix E: A Source Guide — where to find the Ethiopian witnesses and the modern editions.
  • Glossary, Bibliography and Index — terms, sources and a page-number index for the complete volume.
